newsitem.title: USA: U.S. may have to pay utilities to store nuke waste.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may have to pay utilities to store nuke waste.

text.p: A long-simmering battle between the federal government and nuclear power plant owners is set to erupt next year ahead of a 1998 deadline for the government to take over their highly radioactive waste.

With no acceptable central storage facility in sight, the government might have to pay nuclear power plants to keep their spent fuel until the Energy Department builds a dump to bury the waste, utilities and anti-nuclear groups said.

Paying utilities is one of a few options the Energy Department has in light of its decision this week to bow to an appeals court ruling that under a 1982 law the government must take control of spent fuel from commercial power plants by February 1998.
"There's not a whole lot the DOE (Energy Department) can do, because they don't have a place to put the waste," said Bill Magavern of consumer group Public Citizen, opponents of nuclear energy.

The Energy Department has said only that it was reviewing its options. It does not expect to have a dump ready before 2010, assuming its tests on Yucca Mountain in Nevada prove the site is safe for burying radioactive waste for thousands of years.

Storing spent fuel in dry casks at power plants once they start running out of space in pools would cost $34 million to $50 million for a unit which could hold 500 metric tons of uranium, and double that for a 1,000 metric ton unit, according to the Nuclear Energy Institute.
Nuclear plants have generated 32,000 metric tons of spent fuel over the last 40 years, but not all 110 U.S. nuclear plants are expected to run out of storage space before 2010.
Reimbursing utilities for storage costs at their plants would probably entail crediting them for payments into the federal nuclear waste fund from 1998 onward.

About $12 billion has already been paid into the fund by consumers who get their electricity from nuclear plants. They continue to pay into the fund 0.1 cent per kilowatt hour of nuclear power generated, which was meant to cover the costs of building a nuclear waste site by 1998.

"Some arrangement's going to have to be made to maintain the fuel storage in current assemblies," said Joe Maher, spokesman for Duke Power Co., owner of one of nine power stations which has already run out of spent fuel pool space.

"The key issue is can you afford to pay them (utilities) and also have a vigorous site investigation," said an aide to Rep. Edward Markey, D.-Mass., referring to the Energy Department's tests at Yucca Mountain.
Duke Power said it wanted to be involved in any decision which the Energy Department makes.
How the issue is resolved will hinge on the shape of Congress next year.
Any plan is likely to run into competing proposals, backed by utilities, that would require the government to build a temporary storage facility as soon as possible.
The Senate passed a bill in July calling for temporary storage, but the margin was not wide enough to override a veto promised by President Clinton.

Because of the veto threat, the House never voted on similar legislation, which cleared the House Commerce Committee on a strong bipartisan vote, but Republicans are expected to revive the bill early next year.

A lead sponsor of this year's House bill, Republican Rep. Fred Upton of Michigan, said House Speaker Newt Gingrich had promised to schedule the bill early in the new Congress, assuming the Republicans kept control of the House.
"We have the clout in the House to get the bill moving again on both sides of the aisle," Upton said.
Reps. John Dingell of Michigan, top Democrat on the House Commerce Committee, and Frank Pallone, top Democrat on the energy and power subcommittee, both supported Upton's bill this year.
However, Democrats in the House and Senate said interim storage was no longer an option.
"Interim storage is dead," said Sen. Harry Reid of Nevada, who, with Sen. Richard Bryan, also D.-Nev., stirred up vehement opposition to any plan to put a temporary dump in their state.

"Not only do we have President Clinton, we have (Energy Secretary) Hazel O'Leary, (Environmental Protection Agency chief) Carol Browner, (White House chief of staff Leon) Panetta, (Council on Environmental Quality director) Katie McGinty -- their continued opposition to this ridiculous effort to sidetrack permanent storage through this hokey deal for temporary storage," said Reid.
